--- title: "Arctic Fowl" subtitle: "`polars` and `duckplyr`" description: "Interpreted Languages can have nice things too!" date: 07-04-2025 categories: [R, R-Package, Developer-Toolkit] citation: url: https://asenetcky.dev/posts/2025-05-20-thinking-in-projects/ draft: true --- ## What a Time to be Alive In an era where AI is the all the rage, some of the most exciting things I have encountered and have been playing around with lately have been remixes on old favorites. I'm talking of course about working with dataframes. One of my favorites lately has been [polars](https://pola.rs/) and everytime I'd use `polars` and then eventually do some work in R using the [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/), I would really feel some of the niceities in `polars` that were missing in my day-to-day R workflow. This is made all the more apparent to me because I adore working with [dbplyr](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/) and its ability to lazily evaluate R code as sql expressions and `collect()` the results into memory at a time of my choosing. `polars` brings similar asbstractions to the table, however, instead of a sql table being the target, dataframes are. It's a genius idea that has really changed how I work and think about data and what I am capable of doing with both resource rich, and starved computers before needing to scale up to other tools and techniques (if I even need to scale up at all). ... Enter [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/), I've always admired DuckDB from a distance. Dabbling here or there. Some friends and colleagues of mine have thoroughly enjoyed it. I write a bunch of SQL code for work, and for me, it has always felt like that - work. I believe that perhaps this has more to do with the locked down work environment with little to no modern tooling availible to anyone outside of IT (like Data Scientists). However, because of the harsh developer experience when dealing with SQL, I try to do the absolute bare minimum I need to do and bail as fast as possible. So DuckDB just never fell into my lap - until now. [duckplyr](https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2025/06/duckplyr-1-1-0/) joins the `tidyverse` and now we have a fairly seamless drop-in replacement for `dplyr` that leverages a `DuckDB` backend for everything it can, and falls back to regular `dplyr` automatically when handed something it cannot evaluate. For barely any setup at all - you get many of the same bells and whistles of `polars`, but in quite _literally_ a tidy package. Users get their lazy evaluation, their swapping between immediate and deferred execution. Folks can work with data larger than the memory on their computer. Like `polars` there are awesome functions for reading and writing data files. If you're a tidyverse-native like myself, you can do all this without leaving your comfortzone, and why would you want to be anywhere else? In all seriousness, I think this is such an incredible win, `polars` syntax was already fairly similar to `tidyverse` syntax in many ways. There was some cross-over with SQL verbage as well in the `tidyverse`, and DuckDB is in-memory SQL and more. In theory, I now have the ability to be dropped into basically any team working with dataframes, and can just hit the ground running with _good_ options at my disposal regardless of the language of choice and the least amount of impact from context switching. ## Setup You might mutter under your breath: "sure, that is all great, but setup must be a pain" and I would argue no, or at least, it doesn't have to be. Please refer to the documentation for the respective packages, especially as they revolve over time. However, setup might look something like this for most users. ::: {.cell} ::: :::{.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R I'm using `renv` so setup might initially look something like this in the console: ```r renv::install("duckplyr", "dplyr", "conflicted") ``` and then at the top of our R scripts: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(conflicted) library(duckplyr) conflict_prefer("filter", "dplyr") |> suppressMessages() }) ``` ::: ## Python I'm using `uv` for python - so setup in the terminal would look _something_ like this: ```bash $ uv init $ uv add polars ``` and then at the top of our python scripts: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import polars as pl ``` ::: ::: ## Taking a Look If it wasn't obvious before, I want to say this isn't going to be post where I pick a favorite and sell you on it. I really enjoy both packages and programming languages. At the time of writing this, I am primarily an R programmer. I have spent more time with python polars than anything duckdb-related, and quite a bit of time recently with polars. Still, all of the time with python has been considerably less time compared to R. I have experimented a little bit with the duckdb cli tool in the past, but nothing more than an afternoon or two. This is my first real foray into working with the `duckplyr` package. All this to say, that I am not an expert in either of these tools and I am likely not working with them in the most idiomatic way. I'm mostly just here to crush parquet files and have a good time. `duckplyr` has some example data bundled with the package. We'll work with that. First we'll save to parquet file into a temporary folder. In the real world ::: {.callout-note} Ideally, users would just use the data in memory and pass it around between the languages using something like `arrow` and `reticulate` to handle zero-copy streaming etc... However, I think using local files more clearly displays the pros of these packages - so that is the route we're going to take. ::: ### Example Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(fs) my_temp_dir <- fs::file_temp() |> fs::dir_create() data_path <- fs::path(my_temp_dir, "temp-flight-data", ext = "parquet") duckplyr::flights_df() |> duckplyr::compute_parquet(data_path) |> invisible() ``` ::: These data aren't large by any means, but they are readily available - and `duckplyr` uses these data in their documentation. I was able to use 7GB+ parquet files on my humble laptop working with the same code below without crashing my IDE, which is a modern miracle. ### Nanoparquet I want to take a quick aside and mention that `nanoparquet` has some nice tools for inspecting parquets without reading the entire file into memory as well. [nanoparquet](https://nanoparquet.r-lib.org/) is completely dependency free and a worthy companion to `duckplyr`. Since we have a parquet file - let's take a quick peek, and then go back to using the `duckplyr` and `polars`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(nanoparquet) info <- nanoparquet::read_parquet_info(data_path) schema <- nanoparquet::read_parquet_schema(data_path) metadata <- nanoparquet::read_parquet_metadata(data_path) # dimensions and file info head(info) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A data frame: 1 × 7 file_name num_cols num_rows num_row_groups file_size parquet_version * 1 /tmp/Rtmp7qDlpr/fi… 19 336776 3 5813818 1 #
